The checklist is read out loud, item by item.

The route is filed the night before.
An alternate had been named hours earlier.
The fuel was calculated by a second person.
The checklist is read out loud, item by item, on every single flight.
The flight was diverted to the alternate, and the passengers were told.
An alternate airport had been named in the flight plan hours earlier.
The fuel was calculated by a second person, and that is the point.

People think the flying starts when the engines start. It does not. By the time I sit down, the route has already been filed, the fuel has been calculated twice, and an alternate airport has been chosen for me by somebody I have never met. My job in that first half hour is to check work that was done by other people. The checklist is read out loud, item by item, even on the four hundredth flight, and it is read out loud precisely because it is the four hundredth. Nothing on that list is difficult. Everything on it has been forgotten by somebody, once, and that is why it is written down.

The question I get asked most is what happens when the weather closes an airport. The honest answer is that almost nothing is decided in that moment, because almost everything was decided before the aircraft left. An alternate had been named in the flight plan hours earlier. The fuel reserve had been loaded for exactly this. So the flight is diverted, the passengers are told, and it looks like a fast decision from the cabin. It is not. It is a slow decision that was made on paper, and then executed quickly.

The route is filed with air traffic control the night before. The fuel is calculated from the distance, the weather and the weight. The crew is briefed an hour before departure. The checklist is read out loud before the aircraft is moved. Only then is the aircraft cleared for takeoff.
